answers.children: Yes — Sussex Spaniels are good with children because their gentle and affectionate nature combines with a low-slung build that rarely knocks over toddlers. Their determined hunting background gives them patience when following a scent but they can become grumpy if ears are pulled repeatedly. Living with the breed means owners must watch for that stubborn streak around boisterous play. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 7/10)
answers.other-pets: Yes — Sussex Spaniels generally get along with other pets thanks to their gentle temperament and low prey drive developed for flushing rather than chasing game. They show polite sociability toward household animals though same-sex tension can appear if both are strong-willed. The low-to-the-ground spaniel ends up sharing space calmly once introductions are complete.
answers.exercise: Sussex Spaniels need 45 to 60 minutes of daily exercise split into two sessions of steady walking or rambling through wooded areas. Their short legs and endurance from English underbrush hunting mean they prefer sniffing and trudging over running. Without this activity the breed quickly gains weight and turns into a stubborn couch potato.
answers.shedding: Yes — Sussex Spaniels shed moderately year-round with heavier seasonal sheds because their medium double coat traps loose hair in the dense undercoat. The golden-liver texture mats easily around the legs and ears from their low-slung build pushing through wet cover. Owners must brush regularly or the house fills with liver-coloured tumbleweeds.
answers.hypoallergenic: No breed is truly hypoallergenic and the Sussex Spaniel is not one commonly suggested for allergy sufferers. Its medium double coat continues to shed and produce dander despite the affectionate and loyal nature of the dog. The dense coat from its Sussex hunting origins means regular grooming is still required indoors.
answers.training: No — Sussex Spaniels are not easy to train because their determined and stubborn streak makes them independent during sessions. Bred for methodical flushing in dense English underbrush they often follow a scent instead of obeying cues. This leads to slow progress that tests the patience of handlers who expect quick biddability.
answers.lifespan: Sussex Spaniels live 11 to 13 years. Their low-slung build and gentle temperament support steady activity levels but the breed's history of small numbers has left health robustness at a moderate level. Weight gain from their love of comfort can shorten this range if exercise is neglected.
answers.size: Sussex Spaniels reach 35 to 45 lb and stand 13 to 15 in at the shoulder. The compact low-to-the-ground proportions give a solid lumbering feel that fits neatly on a sofa yet remains sturdy enough for muddy field work. Owners enjoy the substantial spaniel presence without the overwhelming bulk of larger sporting breeds.
answers.barking: Sussex Spaniels bark moderately and often use a distinctive bell-like tone to signal when they have found game. Their hunting origins in the wet Sussex hills produced this alert vocalisation rather than constant noise. The sound carries clearly indoors so owners learn to distinguish hunting excitement from everyday fuss.
answers.apartment: Yes — Sussex Spaniels can live in an apartment because their gentle affectionate nature helps them settle indoors after moderate daily walks. The breed's low energy and quiet intensity mean less restless pacing than flashier spaniels though the bell-like bark may disturb thin-walled neighbours. Regular scent games keep them content without a garden.
answers.first-time: No — Sussex Spaniels are not a good first dog because their stubbornness during training demands experienced handling and consistent leadership. The affectionate loyalty emerges only after the owner learns to work with the breed's determined scenting drive rather than against it. Novices often struggle with the slow responses rooted in its methodical English hunting past.
